reasoning: Kept the distinct ellipsis and Spoonerism guidance, and sharpened evidence checking, target identification, and conventional name form. The target wording treats demonstratives and category phrases as cues to resolve what the clue actually requests, rather than imposing a blanket rule that could shift scope. Avoided duplicating existing grammatical-number and qualifier guidance, and made no edits within the protected section. Each edit is supported by one of the two source patches.

edits.target: For fragmentary quotes, titles, nicknames, or familiar sayings and proverbs, infer the omitted word or phrase that completes the clue rather than echoing the supplied text.
edits.content: For fragmentary quotes, titles, nicknames, or familiar sayings and proverbs, infer the omitted word or phrase that completes the clue rather than echoing the supplied text. When an ellipsis marks an unfinished phrase, treat it as a fill-in-the-blank and prefer the missing wording over attribution to a related work or performer that happens to be prominent in context.

edits.target: For compact definition or wordplay clues that give two linked readings, solve the whole clue for the conventional term satisfying both; do not merely restate one reading. Preserve an article when it is part of the expected expression.
edits.content: For Spoonerism clues, restore the intended phrase by reversing the exchanged initial sounds (or other stated sound swaps); answer that intended phrase, not the Spoonerized phrase or a surrounding quotation.

edits.target: Use distinctive details in the question—such as dates, roles, relationships, or defining descriptions—to find evidence that directly explains the full clue, rather than relying on a keyword-only match. If no single passage provides the answer, combine compatible details across relevant passages and corroborate the candidate when evidence is available. Ignore unrelated snippets.
edits.content: Use distinctive details in the question—such as dates, locations, actions, roles, and relationships—to find evidence that explains the full clue, not just a matching keyword. When multiple candidates or related entities appear, test each against all discriminating details and reject candidates that do not fit the complete description. If no single passage provides the answer, combine compatible details across relevant passages and corroborate the candidate when evidence is available. Ignore unrelated snippets.

edits.target: Before choosing a candidate, use the clue's head nouns and pronouns to identify the kind of answer requested: a manner, place, role, institution, species, person, or other category. Return that target, not a consequence, associated entity, or example used to identify it.
edits.content: Before choosing a candidate, use the clue's head nouns, pronouns, and demonstratives to identify the kind of answer requested: a manner, place, role, institution, species, person, or other category. Phrases such as “this play” or “this vitamin” point to the work or substance itself, not its setting or an example. When wording such as “one of these [plural class]” appears, distinguish the class from an individual member and return the entity the clue's grammar actually requests. Return the target, not a consequence or associated entity used to identify it.

edits.target: Use a name form that uniquely identifies the entity: give the complete identifying name when needed, but a surname or shorter form is appropriate when it is unambiguous.
edits.content: Use the context-supported conventional identifying form: include the full name when it is needed or is the canonical form for identifying the entity; use a shorter form only when it is conventionally used and unambiguous.
